data.title: Git
data.tagline: Keep a history of code changes so work can be compared and restored
data.description: Git records snapshots of a project and lets people compare changes, create independent branches, and combine work. Each developer has a full local history. GitHub and similar services host repositories and collaboration, but they are not Git itself.

use: Compare the current work with an earlier state
Collaborate through a shared remote repository
avoid: Commit passwords, tokens, or environment secrets
Treat Git as a backup for generated files and large binaries
Combine unrelated changes in one unclear commit
Run unfamiliar destructive commands without checking the target

lessonPractice.title: The current version works, and an Agent will make a large homepage change next. How should a reliable restore point be created first?

options.label: Duplicate the whole project folder and name it final-version-2
options.feedback: A copy preserves files but does not clearly compare changes and quickly creates ambiguous backup folders.

options.label: Review the current changes and create a clearly described commit before the large edit
options.feedback: A commit records the verified working state in history so later changes can be compared or restored.

options.label: Skip saving a version and run Push to send the current files remotely
options.feedback: Push transfers committed history. Uncommitted working files do not become a restorable version through Push.

data.agentPrompt: Before the large homepage change, inspect git status and the diff, confirm the current version works and contains no secrets, then create a clearly described commit as a restore point. Report its hash and any uncommitted files. Do not push or revert unrelated work.
